Rare founder perspective on navigating AI pricing, talent wars, and model selection while valued at one-third the SaaS peak.

5:11 SaaS valuations halved despite stronger margins; investors misprice growth profiles
Vanta combines historically high margins and rapidly improving growth, yet valuations fell to one-third of peaks. The gap: low-margin AI companies command ten times higher multiples. Christina calls this cognitive dissonance. Investors only fund extremes—lab experiments and early-stage ventures—and avoid mid-stage stable-growth SaaS. Meanwhile, top talent gets poached by higher-valued competitors.

9:18 Token charges fail when customers notice; Vanta absorbs costs and scales adoption
Vanta's agents act autonomously—proposing actions like drafting access-revocation scripts and asking for approval. This consumes enormous token volumes. When Vanta tested token-based billing, customers instantly spotted markups and began comparing raw model performance, forcing Vanta into direct competition with Claude. Rather than mark up tokens, Vanta absorbs the cost, accepts lower margins, and focuses on scaling agent-adoption from 25 percent to 75 percent through better user retention and experience. Pricing strategy comes later.

12:22 Outcome pricing: everyone wants it, nobody can define what counts
Christina, an economist, notes everyone wants outcome-based pricing—where incentives align. The problem: what's an outcome? Closing a support ticket is output; real outcome is solving the customer's problem. Even retreating to ticket closure, forty-plus measurable units exist: draft documents, close alerts, revoke accounts, etc. Users can't calculate what each agent action should cost. Result: every company wants outcome pricing but nobody can implement it, so they use point-to-token ratios that smart users see through.

14:27 Agents need modular codebases; eight-year-old systems need architectural rewrites
Agents work better on modular codebases—it's a token-context problem. Vanta's eight-year-old codebase required a year of modularization so agents could understand whole modules instead of drowning in legacy code. Otherwise an expert needs to monitor the agent constantly, defeating the purpose. Christina frames this as an old problem amplified: new engineers used to need ramp time; now Vanta wants 9,000 instant agent engineers. She grades herself low on this work.

19:40 Teams ship proven patterns over risky LLM, unless explicitly forbidden
When Vanta redesigned customer onboarding, the team kept proposing a four-step progress wizard despite feedback to use LLM. The blocker: they felt "not allowed to fail" on this project. The wizard was proven; the LLM approach risked failure. Once leadership explicitly said "this must succeed," the team shipped an LLM-based solution the next day—and it worked well. Christina didn't anticipate this psychological blocker.

23:46 Top talent compensation jumped tenfold in five years; still undervalued
On talent wars, Christina notes that compensation bands are a joke—the real band is whatever competitors offer. For the same role, total compensation has grown roughly tenfold compared to five years ago, and she thinks it should be higher. Her philosophy: you never pay top talent enough. She describes their qualities—high agency, execution, deep business understanding, sound judgment, iteration—as worth millions, yet they sound like clichés. The only force keeping salary growth in check is investor worry about equity dilution, but that concern is nearly gone now.

33:01 French companies chose Chinese models to hedge against supply cuts
During recent Paris customer visits, Christina found that many French software companies now primarily use Chinese AI models. She initially guessed nationalism, but the real reason: after Trump blocked certain models for non-US users, companies realized their business continuity risk. No guarantee US models stay available. So they switched to Chinese models wholesale. Not values—risk management.

52:40 Losing the billboard to a cash-rich startup signals market shift
Vanta's iconic billboard at the 101/280 interchange, famous for "compliance that doesn't suck too much," got stolen during renewal by a competitor—Vanta only had a placement order, no long-term contract. Christina offered double, then triple the price, but the competitor said "we have positive cash flow" and wouldn't sell. Vanta lost the location. She joked it felt like watching market capitalization decline in real time.

item.title: CME CEO: 2,500 regulatory filings all approved, not a single rejection
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-20-oddlots-芝商所ceo-两千五百份监管申报全部通过-一个没被拒绝/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-20-oddlots-芝商所ceo-两千五百份监管申报全部通过-一个没被拒绝/
item.description: The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission has rejected zero of nearly 2,500 new product filings, approving everything from ‘how many hot dogs can Joey Chestnut eat’ to ‘whether George Santos attends the State of the Union’—CME CEO Terry Duffy says this amounts to regulation existing in name only.
item.content:encoded:
The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission has rejected zero of nearly 2,500 new product filings, approving everything from ‘how many hot dogs can Joey Chestnut eat’ to ‘whether George Santos attends the State of the Union’—CME CEO Terry Duffy says this amounts to regulation existing in name only.

Want to understand how US financial regulation gets circumvented and where the legal boundaries lie for perpetual contracts and prediction markets—this episode is dense with information.

1:02 46-year veteran hands off but doesn't fully step away
Duffy has worked at CME for 46 years, starting at $56 per week, and became chairman when CME went public in 2002. Next year he will transition to executive chairman and hand the CEO title to Lynn Fitzpatrick, but emphasizes he will stay to help her through the initial transition period and will intervene if necessary.

4:05 When regulators approve everything: 2,500 filings, zero rejections
Since the second Trump administration took office, Duffy says, 2,500 self-certified filings submitted to the CFTC have been rejected zero times—including prediction contracts on ‘how many hot dogs can Joey Chestnut eat’ and betting on ‘whether George Santos shows up at the State of the Union’. He believes these contracts obviously violate Core Principle 3 (susceptibility to manipulation), yet regulators pass everything through without question.

6:06 Regulation by executive order evaporates when the administration changes
Duffy points out that the CFTC and SEC now rely on many new rules sidestepping congressional legislation, with agencies writing their own regulations unilaterally—rules that the next administration can wipe away with a pen stroke, just as Trump did with Biden's executive orders after taking office. He argues this is not sustainable regulation; good regulation must survive any change of government.

11:11 Perpetual contracts are swaps—and CME refuses to play that game
Duffy explains that perpetual contracts use funding rates to make long and short positions pay each other to peg the contract to spot prices. Under Dodd-Frank, anything involving mutual payments between counterparties should be classified as a swap, not a futures contract. Futures get the favorable 60/40 long/short-term tax treatment under Section 1256; swaps are taxed as ordinary income and must be cleared and registered within five days. For this reason, CME abandoned launching a 24-hour crude oil perpetual contract and instead launched only a regular 24-hour crude oil mini futures contract.

15:20 Hyperliquid skips KYC—Duffy calls it a Core Principle 9 violation
In response to Hyperliquid founder Jeff Yan's earlier claim on the show that ‘the platform doesn't need to be regulated, the deployer does,’ Duffy counters that the platform itself has not implemented KYC (know your customer) and nobody is reviewing who is trading or what leverage they're using—he notes that leverage products on Hyperliquid can reach 250%, making a move of one or two points enough to trigger cascading liquidations. He argues this violates Core Principle 9, which requires exchanges to surveil their own markets, and if Hyperliquid wants to operate compliantly in the US, it must follow US law.

20:33 GPU futures blocked as national security threat—Duffy isn't buying it
Duffy says the GPU market is already over one trillion dollars and is expected by 2030 to be several times the size of the crypto asset class (currently under $3 trillion), but the government has shelved GPU futures products on national security grounds—a rationale he finds incomprehensible. If the US government truly wants to lead in AI and data centers, it should let the industry use futures to hedge GPU-related risks instead of indefinitely strangling this product category.

22:33 24/7 trading is inevitable—but the banking system is the bottleneck
Duffy believes 24/7 trading is inevitable, but the biggest obstacle is the banking system—banks close after Friday and no one can fund a full week ahead for the $76 trillion US equity market over the weekend. The crypto market is small enough that CME already runs full-time trading, but interest rates and equity products must wait for the banking system to go 24/7 as well. As an interim step, CME plans to expand equity trading hours to 23.5 hours by year-end.

25:35 More frightening than 2008: the day oil went negative
When asked about the scariest moment in his career, Duffy says negative oil prices during the COVID pandemic in 2020 terrified him more than the 2008 financial crisis. On April 20, 2020, he went on television defending WTI crude crashing to negative $37.50, and faced public outrage. What truly frightened him was that there was nowhere to store the physical product and demand evaporated instantly, with no idea how long the condition would persist.

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-20-tpwky-fda换掉审查委员后-被警示有风险的肽类产品照样获批/
item.description: A scientific review panel unanimously flagged seven popular peptides as unsafe, but RFK's replacement committee nearly unanimously approved them—laying bare the gap between regulatory science and political appointment.
item.content:encoded:
A scientific review panel unanimously flagged seven popular peptides as unsafe, but RFK's replacement committee nearly unanimously approved them—laying bare the gap between regulatory science and political appointment.

Not a generic science explainer on peptide risks, but a dissection of the gray market's regulatory loopholes, money trails, and real harm cases documented behind each popular peptide.

8:35 The word "peptide" itself is meaningless
Peptide is chemically just "a chain of amino acids"—oxytocin, insulin, most hormones and neurotransmitters are all peptides. The speaker finds the term's overuse deeply frustrating because asking "do you eat peptides" is meaningless, like asking "do you eat molecules." The real questions should be about which specific peptide, whether there is human safety data, and whether this dose and route have been researched, not treating a chemical classification as a unified wellness concept.

14:45 Peptide drugs have been in medical use for a century
Humans first used peptides as medicine in 1921 with insulin, extracted from cow and pig pancreas, saving millions of lives. Scientists cracked synthetic peptides in the 1950s, with another breakthrough in 1984—both won Nobel prizes in chemistry. By 2021 FDA had approved 80 peptide drugs for diabetes, weight loss, osteoporosis, cancer, HIV, and multiple sclerosis. The novelty is not that "peptides work as medicine"—it is that the versions now sold online never went through this approval process.

19:57 Unregulated peptide market ads grew eightfold in four years
These peptides sold via WhatsApp, direct from Chinese factories, labeled "for research use only" are neither prescription drugs nor compliant supplements—pure gray market. The New York Times reported that web ads for unauthorized peptide products grew eightfold from 2022 to 2024. An industry report valued the 2022 global peptide market at $37.8 billion, projected to grow 9% annually and reach $85.9 billion by 2031—a multi-billion-dollar industry that skipped clinical trials and FDA approval.

24:02 GLP-1's success created a halo effect for all peptides
Semaglutide and tirzepatide are themselves peptides, and their weight-loss success brought "peptide" into mass consciousness for the first time. The halo effect: once you see benefits in one domain, you assume they exist everywhere, so "this new peptide is amazing" expands to "all peptides are worth trying." GLP-1 drugs also normalized self-injection as a path to self-improvement. Early scarcity pushed people to buy outside legitimate channels, paving the way for the gray market.

30:10 Experts unanimously warned against these peptides; the committee approved them anyway
In 2023 FDA removed 12 peptides from the "503A bulks list" (which compounding pharmacies can use) due to insufficient safety evidence. RFK Jr. tweeted about ending FDA's "oppression" of peptides; after becoming HHS secretary, he replaced 8 members of the committee responsible for reviewing this list. At July's hearing, the scientific review panel raised significant safety concerns about all 7 re-examined peptides and found insufficient efficacy evidence for any. Yet all but one were voted back onto the list—votes almost always 8 in favor, 6 opposed, 1 abstaining.

39:31 Wolverine stack has zero human data and cancer-promoting mechanisms
The most popular combo, "Wolverine stack," consists of BPC-157 and TB-500, claimed to accelerate recovery. Neither has real human safety data—BPC-157 has only one small 17-person study, TB-500 has zero human research and no toxicity data. More troubling: TB-500 derives from TB4, which promotes blood vessel growth, cell proliferation, and blocks cell death—precisely what tumors excel at. People are literally injecting themselves with potentially cancer-promoting compounds.

46:43 Barbie peptide has already caused cancer and muscle breakdown
Melanotan-2, called "Barbie peptide," claims to darken skin and boost libido by stimulating melanin receptors, directly activating skin-cancer-related pathways. It has already caused cancer in at least two reported cases, plus rhabdomyolysis and kidney infarction. At a Las Vegas wellness expo, people injecting unknown peptides were hospitalized; one was intubated. These are not hypothetical risks—they are documented cases of real harm already recorded in medical literature.

49:48 When the patent became public, counterfeits flooded the gray market
Retatrutide is Eli Lilly's Phase 3 drug targeting three weight-loss hormones with impressive clinical data. Because clinical data is published and patents are public, the amino acid sequence is findable; companies copied it and sold it on the gray market. Buyers do not know if they are getting the real thing or correct doses. People are rapidly losing weight on counterfeit unapproved drugs with no doctor supervision—explicitly described as extremely dangerous.

item.category: Ask Lisa: The Psychology of Raising Tweens & Teens
item.description: A seventh-grader's group Halloween costume dispute looks like a wardrobe disagreement on the surface, but is really a fight over who gets left out and who holds social power—the costume is just the container that puts this negotiation on the table.
item.content:encoded:
A seventh-grader's group Halloween costume dispute looks like a wardrobe disagreement on the surface, but is really a fight over who gets left out and who holds social power—the costume is just the container that puts this negotiation on the table.

If your kid is being squeezed out by a friend group chat or is falling apart over costume disagreement, this episode gives you specific questions to ask and how to set boundaries in group chats—not just a "don't worry about it."

2:02 Costume Fights Are Never Just About Costumes
One seventh-grader and four close friends do a group Halloween costume every year; this year, by September, they're already fighting. Two want to dress as one character group, one says no—not that costume. Screenshots of the group chat circulate. The daughter feels quietly kicked out of the plan even though no one's actually said it. Tori says this isn't a Halloween problem—it's a bigger negotiation over who decides things and who gets included. The costume is just what brings it to the surface.

6:18 Why Halloween Night Gets Uniquely Overloaded
They use the psychology term overdetermination to describe Halloween: the night compresses several identity shifts—is she still young enough to knock on doors for candy, or old enough to think of this as freedom to roam without parents? The costume itself splits between "sexy" and "funny." Does she want to join boys in the group? All these adolescent crossroads collide on one night and explode—way more complex than adults realize.

9:27 Helping Isn't the Same as Fixing It for Them
Parents' first instinct is often to just opt out—"let's skip group costumes, do your own thing"—but to the kid that reads as "switch schools"–level rejection. It denies what she actually wants: to stay in the group. Tori's frame is "helping without fixing": start with empathy ("this sucks"), not a solution, because there's no answer that satisfies everyone. The goal is support, not to make the conflict disappear.

15:45 There Are Two Kinds of Popular—and They Mean Opposite Things
Tori splits "popular" into two: kids who are actually liked, and kids who buy social power by being mean—everyone knows it but no one dares push back. Helping your kid name which kind of "power" is actually running this friend group is the key to understanding what the costume fight is really about. Lisa emphasizes this clinical insight again at the end.

20:59 Group Chat Groupthink Is Worse Than Individual Judgment
Psychology shows group thinking usually spirals worse than any one person would decide alone—it drifts toward either meaner or dumber. In group chats, no one dares step out or object, so everyone ends up passively part of cruelty they don't actually endorse but can't say out loud.

23:00 A Teen Brain's Brakes Aren't Installed Yet
The part of the brain that asks "should I send this, will it get screenshotted and spread?" isn't done developing during adolescence, so group chat messages go out of control at a word. Real guidance isn't writing the text for them—it's repeatedly asking "if you said that, what do you think would happen?"—letting them rehearse consequences in their head. Even if she doesn't answer, that rehearsal is happening.

28:15 When the Group Chat Spirals, a Parent Can Take the Fall
If the chat crosses a line, Tori says set the boundary and let the kid tell her friends "my mom made me leave the chat"—let her blame the parent and use that as a way out of a confrontation she's not ready for. That's not teaching her to lie; it's giving a kid who isn't ready to face the group a face-saving exit. The day she can say "stop, this is wrong" will come naturally—don't force it now.

33:26 High School Homecoming and Seventh-Grade Costumes Come from the Same Root
Zoom out to sophomore and junior year homecoming fights: the same social power is still there, just split among more people as friend groups loosen. The parent role shifts from front-line involved to informed but hands-off. This says the costume conflict itself will pass, but the social structure that shaped it stays, just in different forms.

item.title: The polygraph doesn't test lies, it tests the fear that makes you confess
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-20-throughline-测谎仪不测谎-测的是让人认罪的心理恐惧/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-20-throughline-测谎仪不测谎-测的是让人认罪的心理恐惧/
item.description: US courts rejected the polygraph's science, yet allowed police to use it to extract confessions—its value was never detecting lies, but manufacturing confessions and ongoing surveillance through psychological fear.
item.content:encoded:
US courts rejected the polygraph's science, yet allowed police to use it to extract confessions—its value was never detecting lies, but manufacturing confessions and ongoing surveillance through psychological fear.

Traces the polygraph from its invention through legal restrictions, explaining where workplace and job-screening polygraph requirements came from.

1:01 First case solved, suspect may never have been guilty
The 1921 Berkeley theft case where police used a polygraph on a female suspect, who panicked and fled, then confessed after days of continued surveillance. The inventor Larson later doubted her guilt—she had psychological issues and the thefts continued afterward. This "first solved case" suggests the polygraph's value wasn't finding the truth, but extracting confession through humiliation and pressure.

9:41 The polygraph was invented to monitor police, not criminals
Created in 1920s Berkeley by August Vollmer (the "father of modern policing") and physiologist John Larson to civilize brutal police practices. The first people systematically polygraphed were Berkeley police themselves—the tool was used for internal accountability to prove police weren't breaking the law, building public trust in the technology before use on suspects.

11:44 Courts banned polygraph evidence while police kept using it in interrogation rooms
In United States v. Frye, a murder suspect confessed then recanted; the polygraph showed innocence but the judge barred the jury from hearing it. The case established the Frye rule: only evidence vetted by the scientific community is admissible in court. But police continued using polygraphs to pressure suspects in interrogation rooms—police are legally permitted to lie and use deception to elicit statements that can later be introduced in court, regardless of the polygraph's scientific validity.

14:56 The polygraph became a tool for continuous employee surveillance in corporate America
Leonard Keeler, a colleague of Larson's, brought the polygraph to Chicago in the 1930s and sold testing services to banks and retailers like Walgreens. Found that employees often confessed to small thefts during tests. When management wanted to fire them, Keeler advised against it: knowing they could be polygraphed anytime made these employees the most honest. The tool transformed from a crime-solving instrument into a system of continuous workplace surveillance, spreading through banking, retail, and federal agencies.

16:00 Large-scale polygraph screening creates impossible statistical problems
When used at Los Alamos and Oak Ridge on thousands of nuclear weapons project employees, Ken Alder points out that even if the polygraph worked perfectly (it doesn't), mass screening produces enormous false positives—all the innocent people get investigated while actual liars slip through. The tool might have some value for a single suspect, but applied to an entire workforce, the mathematics breaks down entirely.

17:01 A Secretary of State threatened resignation to ban workplace polygraphs
From the 1960s onward, unions and the public opposed polygraph abuse; by the 1980s about half the states had banned it in employment. But it remained legal federally. When Reagan wanted to use polygraphs to hunt leakers in government, Secretary of State George Shultz declared it scientifically worthless and threatened to resign. This prompted Congress and Reagan to sign the Employee Polygraph Protection Act in 1988, banning private-sector employee testing, though government security, police, and pharmaceuticals were exempted. Industry scale collapsed from its peak.

19:10 The polygraph masks subjectivity with the false objectivity of technology
Ken Alder frames this as a very American story, like the SAT—seemingly machine-scored, objective, and fair, yet SAT is criticized for hidden bias. The polygraph is the same: who determines if someone is lying isn't the machine but the operator's subjective reading of the waveforms. The belief that "a neutral machine can solve social problems" is itself a distinctly American myth.

20:14 The polygraph may create nothing more than security theater
Alder concludes the problem isn't just that polygraphs don't detect lies, but that they create "security theater"—like airport metal detectors, giving false reassurance while not actually improving safety. He closes with Montaigne's 450-year-old observation: truth has one face, but liars have a thousand; extracting truth from someone's mind is a game that's hard to win.

item.title: A Lithography Machine Still Approved for Export Could Let China Match U.S. Chip Capacity in a Decade
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-20-chinatalk-一款仍在放行的光刻机-可能在十年内让中国芯片产能追平美国/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-20-chinatalk-一款仍在放行的光刻机-可能在十年内让中国芯片产能追平美国/
item.description: U.S. think tanks calculate that if a submersion lithography machine continues to be permitted for export, China's chip production capacity could approach or even match America's within ten years; if supplies are cut off entirely, that possibility closes permanently.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. think tanks calculate that if a submersion lithography machine continues to be permitted for export, China's chip production capacity could approach or even match America's within ten years; if supplies are cut off entirely, that possibility closes permanently.

This is a rare deep-read interpretation of a report that lays bare the mechanics of lithography machine export controls—for anyone who wants to understand the concrete mechanics of U.S.-China chip competition, not slogans.

7:17 The overlooked deep-UV already supports production of Huawei's Ascend chips
Public attention focuses on EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography, with single machines selling for hundreds of millions of dollars and viewed as the world's most advanced technology—China still cannot import any. But DUV (deep ultraviolet) lithography, though one generation behind, still costs $60–80 million per unit, and its most advanced models can fully support the process nodes required by flagship AI chips like Huawei's Ascend. In other words, the outside world thinks ‘blocking EUV wins the game,’ but the technology actually supporting China's domestically produced AI chip lines is the DUV model still approved for export.

11:47 Export controls left a crater-sized loophole
Current U.S. rules permit China to import the NXT:1980 submersion DUV lithography machine from ASML—enough to support 7-nanometer logic and HBM2E/HBM3-class memory manufacturing, exactly matching Huawei Ascend's requirements. Nick describes this opening as ‘not a loophole but a crater’: between 2024 and 2025 alone, China imported roughly 90 of these systems for over $10 billion, accounting for nearly two-thirds of ASML's total submersion DUV exports.

14:52 Continuing to permit exports could let China match U.S. capacity within a decade
Based on current lithography machine inventory and process physics constraints, even if China redirected all its systems to AI chips and manufactured not a single mobile phone chip, by 2035 its capacity would almost certainly stay below one-tenth of America's—an advantage nearly locked in. But if China maintains its 2024–2025 import pace and redirects a larger share of capacity from consumer electronics to AI chips (the ‘AI-first’ scenario), the production curve in ten years could bend toward matching or even approaching U.S. levels, and the certainty around the global compute landscape disappears.

24:21 The MATCH Act aims to align allies' controls with U.S. standards
The MATCH Act pursues two things: first, elevate several categories of ‘high-lethality’ equipment, including submersion DUV lithography machines, from controls targeting specific entities like SMIC and Changxin Memory to a complete countrywide ban on China; second, align Japan and the Netherlands' controls on all semiconductor manufacturing equipment with the standard America already enforces—the U.S. already prohibits ‘not a single device’ from reaching advanced Chinese production lines, while allies have not reached that level. The bill gives the Commerce Department 150 days to negotiate with allies; if talks fail, it authorizes unilateral action.

32:33 Whether cutting off service will actually choke production is anyone's guess
The bill also aims to cut off on-site maintenance by ASML and Tokyo Electron engineers in China. But Nick admits this is the most opaque corner of the entire research: many maintenance engineers are Chinese contract workers, and some spare parts are locally manufactured in China, so a supply cut may not immediately force the engineers out. His assessment: equipment won't stop dead, but once core subsystems—light sources, wafer stages, sensors—lose OEM support, yield and capacity will likely begin eroding slowly over 6–12 months, with degradation accelerating over time.

41:44 Congressional legislation is harder to reverse under pressure than executive order
Some worry about a replay of summer 2025: China plays the rare-earth card, and the Trump administration is forced to back down. But Nick sees a difference: export controls are executive orders—the President signs, it's done, the leverage stays at the White House. Once written into law by Congress, even if a given administration wanted to delay, the statute itself remains, and a successor could enforce it again. More crucial: the bite of an import ban unfolds over 3–10 years—a slow variable, unlike tariffs that hurt export-driven economies immediately next week, and governments cave easiest to ‘pain this week,’ not pain in 2030.

1:05:00 The U.S. and Japan together can lock down DUV without invoking long-arm jurisdiction
Even if the Dutch government refuses to cooperate, America has a quiet alternative: DUV light-source subsystems come from only two companies—Cymer (U.S.) and Gigaphoton (Japan)—and Cymer is now ASML's subsidiary. If the U.S. and Japan each pass legislation stipulating ‘this light source cannot flow to China's submersion DUV systems,’ there's no need to invoke FDPR or long-arm jurisdiction; the two countries can jointly choke off all submersion DUV exports to China, even if the machines themselves are Dutch.

1:08:12 Lithography machines rank first among tools in U.S.-China strategic competition
When asked ‘should we prioritize cutting off China's remote access to U.S. computing capacity?’, Nick's ranking is clear: in the medium to long term, lithography machines rank first. Not because their impact on capacity is biggest, but because the leverage is different—when China rents overseas compute, America can cut it off instantly; once China owns its own chip lines, that leverage vanishes. His view: true strategic advantage rests on autonomous chip manufacturing, and autonomous chip manufacturing rests on lithography machines.

item.title: Astra takes robots into their GPT moment—but AI pharma hits the validation wall
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-19-sv101-astra让机器人一步跨进gpt时刻-却在ai制药撞上验证墙/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-19-sv101-astra让机器人一步跨进gpt时刻-却在ai制药撞上验证墙/
item.description: Robots achieve a qualitative leap through self-reflection and iteration, but while AI can design molecules in hours, real validation depends on mice and monkey metabolic cycles—a wall no model can cross.
item.content:encoded:
Robots achieve a qualitative leap through self-reflection and iteration, but while AI can design molecules in hours, real validation depends on mice and monkey metabolic cycles—a wall no model can cross.

Three frontline practitioners in robotics, agents, and AI pharma break down—with concrete figures—what has genuinely advanced one month after Astra's launch versus what remains demo-stage hype.

4:05 Astra converts chain-of-thought reflection directly into physical action
Past robot models and language models only reflected at the linguistic level, but Astra can turn this chain-of-thought reasoning into actual motor commands. Xu Huazhe describes it hitting a table, then saying ‘the table is quite high, should I lift my hand higher?’ and actually adjusting. It iterates: drawing the Golden Gate Bridge poorly at first, refining it over rounds into photographic accuracy; encountering an unfamiliar obstacle like plant stems splitting in a vase, it figures out to pinch the fork point before inserting. This ability to cross from language-level reflection into physical generalization across domains was unavailable in previous robot models.

16:07 Meta Muse's browser automation is retracing Manus's path—toward collision with platforms
Meta Muse operates by giving each user a cloud virtual machine to control browsers for shopping, travel, and customer service. But Manus walked this exact road first. Platforms like Amazon quickly block this class of IP traffic, forcing Manus to pivot toward white-collar productivity tools. Bill Zhu observes that most third-party platforms won't open APIs; agents must masquerade as regular users to bypass detection. This friction is inevitable, the confrontation will repeat, and consumer-facing agents aren't mature enough to win yet.

19:10 Merchants don't block agents—they block unverified identity
Bill Zhu identifies a critical insight: merchants aren't afraid of agents per se, but of cloud VMs they can't verify as the actual user. If one user maps to one agent, merchants accept it. But if a single person deploys 20 agents to price-compare and game traffic, the merchant's funnel is effectively hijacked. For consumer agents to break through, the solution requires a hardware-software hybrid: only agents running on the user's own device carry trustworthy identity. Only then will merchants grant access.

22:13 Astra costs 4–5× more than GPT-6 Sol—the token-burn war is just beginning
Astra's pricing: $10 per million input tokens, $50 per million output tokens—4 to 5 times the cost of GPT-6 Sol. Bill Zhu's personal experience: he burned through his 20× Claude subscription allowance on a single task, then spent an extra $100 in credits, all consumed within 2–3 agent conversation turns. Routing even 10% of Meta Muse's traffic to Astra-tier models would be catastrophic. This is why he predicts the consumer-agent token war will be extraordinarily brutal, with competitors like Instinct facing steep customer acquisition costs.

26:14 The real token sink isn't chat—it's solving unsolved science problems
A frontier-model researcher explains that consumer-agent conversations don't burn many tokens; inference costs keep dropping. The true token sink—and the arena where OpenAI, Claude, and DeepMind compete most fiercely internally—is AI for Science: problems with no established solutions. When OpenAI solved the Navier–Stokes equation, a single agent run sent 2.7 million messages, consuming roughly 1.3 billion output tokens, valued at ~$22 million retail price per attempt. Most users sense no gap between Astra and prior generations. Frontier scientists perceive a monumental capability jump.

43:25 Dual-arm tasks defeat Astra—it can't learn to improve with repetition
After weeks of intensive testing, Xu Huazhe identified Astra's limits. Dual-arm coordination nearly fails; clothes-folding, a task hard to describe precisely, it cannot perform. A sharper constraint: it doesn't improve through practice. First attempt: one hour. Second attempt: 45 minutes. Third attempt and beyond: frozen at 45 minutes, never shrinking further—unlike humans or smaller native robot models that compress execution time to seconds through training. Robots have entered their GPT moment, yet fine-grained dexterity and continuous self-improvement remain open problems for end-to-end models.

47:26 AI prescribes drugs but can't design protocols for your lab's equipment
Wang Sheng notes: today's models can predict protein activity and suggest molecular candidates. What's missing—and most critical in biomedics—is forcing AI to generate a concrete, executable lab protocol: exact temperature, specific molecules, humidity levels, timing. It's like asking Astra to cook using only your kitchen's tomatoes, eggs, and potatoes—yet it designs a seafood feast. The model doesn't understand and won't adapt to available hardware and resources. His estimate: models reach maybe 30% completion on experiment design; human experts must revise repeatedly. No model can seal this gap.

56:31 AlphaFold went open-source but created a moat around proprietary data
AlphaFold's open release sparked a wave of AI pharma startups, most unsuccessful. Even with molecule design compressed from six months to hours, real-world validation on mice and monkeys still stalls the pipeline. Wang Sheng observes that open-sourcing shifted what matters: the community now races to accumulate data. Genuine animal-experiment data is worth $10,000 to $100,000+ per trial, invisible in internet corpora. Once tools open, companies holding wet-lab datasets gain deeper moats. Anthropic's strategy exemplifies this: directly partnering with wet-lab firm Adaptyv Bio, binding benchmark results to live validation. Data—not models—became the actual competitive advantage.

item.title: AI didn't raise creativity's ceiling—people pushing boldly did

item.description: Figma founder admits he was wrong when he predicted AI would raise the ceiling on creativity. AI only lowers the barrier to making things; only people bold enough to take real risks actually raise the ceiling.
item.content:encoded:
Figma founder admits he was wrong when he predicted AI would raise the ceiling on creativity. AI only lowers the barrier to making things; only people bold enough to take real risks actually raise the ceiling.

The first 20 minutes cover the Adobe acquisition story with moderate density; after 20 minutes, his argument about AI and the creativity ceiling becomes the episode's most valuable section.

3:03 Regulators killed a $20 billion deal by applying yesterday's market logic
Figma and Adobe signed a $20 billion acquisition agreement, but US, EU, and UK CMA regulators intervened on antitrust grounds, dragging out the review for 16 months. Dylan argues the regulators applied yesterday's market definitions to a market being redefined by AI right now. He cites the Roomba-Amazon case as a cautionary tale: FTC blocked it, Roomba eventually failed, and the market flowed to China—suggesting that antitrust intervention can harm the very competition it aims to protect.

10:09 Losing certainty gave 1,200 employees the one thing they needed most
The agreement collapsed on the first day of a company holiday. Dylan called an all-hands video meeting on Monday afternoon to announce the news. Employees' first reaction was not disappointment but relief—finally, they didn't have to live in uncertainty anymore. He then opened an exit door: if anyone had joined Figma only hoping to eventually work at Adobe, and wanted to leave, the company would pay them several months' salary with no hard feelings. The only condition was waiting six months before reapplying. In the end, only a small fraction chose to leave.

14:16 New models disrupted design software; product moat won anyway
After Anthropic released Claude Design, the market immediately declared Figma dead. But Figma's next quarterly report showed 48 percent year-over-year revenue growth, bucking the prediction entirely. Dylan's explanation: the market conflated "model progress" with "product progress." Professional design tools like Figma have deep moats built on years of workflow refinement—not on underlying model capability. A new model-powered competitor struggles to replicate that accumulated expertise overnight.

17:18 Cursor proved indie teams beat tech giants through sheer focus
Dylan cites Cursor as proof. By all rights it shouldn't have won—at the stage when Cursor lacked its own model, cutting-edge AI labs with in-house models were chasing the same lane. But Cursor obsessed over user experience and kept polishing product details, and it won anyway. His conclusion: SaaS isn't binary—"either everyone dies or everyone thrives." As long as you deeply understand your users and stay focused, small teams can still break through even with giants circling.

20:30 AI raised the floor of entry, not the ceiling of creation
Dylan admits he was wrong years ago when he said at Figma's Config conference that "AI will raise the ceiling of creativity." Now he sees it differently: AI only lowers the barrier to getting things made, letting more people produce more content. But the ceiling itself hasn't moved up by a millimeter. Only humans raise the ceiling—those willing to invest time, take real risks, and attempt something no one has ever done before.

24:33 Labeling AI-written work creates trust only for human-crafted contributions
Figma has a simple internal rule: anything written with AI must be labeled "written with AI" at the top of the document. Dylan says this started as a light joke, but people actually follow it. He sees it creating a trust hierarchy inside the organization—knowing that something was carefully hand-crafted by a person carries more weight, and that trust is the reward for doing things with your own hands.

32:43 AI excels where truth is verifiable; design remains a human domain
Dylan observes that models in verifiable, formal domains like mathematics and cybersecurity are stacking up capabilities at breakneck speed. But in creative and design domains—where you can't verify correctness—progress has been merely incremental. This might actually reveal humanity's remaining role in the AI toolkit: people brainstorm and design; AI executes more of the work. Design and creativity remain fundamentally human acts.

38:06 Solving 700 math problems solves away something precious and irreplaceable
The night before recording, OpenAI released over 700 papers cracking famous unsolved math problems. Dylan called it "perhaps the greatest day of discovery in human history," but admitted a certain melancholy underneath—as if humanity gained something and lost something at once. The mystery and wonder of these mathematical puzzles is being stripped away and solved. There's triumph in it, and a tinge of loss.

item.title: AI didn't break critical thinking education—it was never taught well to begin with

item.description: Critical thinking education was already failing; AI simply exposed the problem sooner. The only evidence-supported solution isn't to ban AI—it's to preserve the productive friction in learning.
item.content:encoded:
Critical thinking education was already failing; AI simply exposed the problem sooner. The only evidence-supported solution isn't to ban AI—it's to preserve the productive friction in learning.

This episode tests the worry that 'AI makes people dumb' against real evidence—sorting what's confirmed from what's still speculation, plus concrete, actionable learning strategies.

1:02 An AI system can now teach an entire course solo
Tsinghua University education researcher Li Xiang Yin initially wanted to use the agentic AI tool Codex to help build an online course. Instead, he discovered the AI was sophisticated enough to independently complete all assignments, answer questions, and participate in discussions—students could pass without any intellectual effort. This made him realize that teaching students to reason and think through things is now more critical than ever. This isn't an isolated case: a 2025 survey of over 1,000 US university educators found that 90% believe generative AI will weaken students' critical thinking. A separate global survey found that about 20% of students using AI report they struggle more with problem-solving when they don't have it.

4:05 Critical thinking skills stop working when you switch fields
Critical thinking is often treated as a transferable, general-purpose skill, but cognitive psychologist Daniel Willingham and others emphasize it only works when tied to domain-specific knowledge. One study found that neurologists perform poorly diagnosing cardiology cases—even though neurology and cardiology are both medicine, the thinking methods don't transfer directly. This means teaching critical thinking can't be done in abstract terms divorced from specific subjects: history demands comparing archives and artifacts, while science requires understanding the relationships between theory, hypothesis, method, and evidence. These aren't the same skill set.

5:05 Using AI boosts test scores—until you take it away
A 2024 study gave middle schoolers ChatGPT-like generative AI tools to solve math problems. Their performance improved while using AI. But when the AI was removed, their scores dropped below students who had never used AI at all. Researcher Yin argues AI works both ways—it can enhance learning if used well, or erode ability if used as a shortcut. The critical variable is how the task is designed: if AI just delivers ready-made answers, students don't have to think; if AI forces students to generate their own feedback and solve problems themselves, the result is completely different.

6:06 Given a choice, students abandon thinking tools for shortcuts
Yin designed an AI specifically intended to force students to reason first—the goal was to make them work through problems before seeing answers. But he observed that some students simply turned off this AI and switched to ChatGPT to get ready-made answers. 'This is a bit shocking, but that's the reality, isn't it?' he said. This reveals that even when well-designed learning tools are available, people naturally gravitate toward the path of least resistance rather than actively choosing the harder but more effective approach. This is precisely the friction researchers repeatedly worry about—the friction AI removes.

9:06 Only metacognition among teaching strategies has solid evidence
Among the many approaches to teaching critical thinking, metacognition—reflection on, planning for, and monitoring of one's own learning process—is one of the few with solid empirical support. The UK Education Endowment Foundation (EEF), drawing on a systematic literature review, estimates that teaching students metacognitive strategies is among the most effective tools schools can deploy, delivering on average the equivalent of eight months of additional learning progress per year. By contrast, critical thinking itself still lacks standardized assessment tools. The OECD is partnering with a London-based education company to develop such an assessment specifically for middle and high school students; the project involves about 800 school teachers testing the materials.

11:07 Finding an answer online doesn't mean you understand it
Young people spend considerable time on social media but systematically overestimate their ability to spot misinformation. A survey of nearly 24,000 college students in the Philippines found that 63% believed they could identify fake news, but when actually tested, only 26% could. Researchers developed two teaching approaches based on these findings: one is inoculation—exposing students in advance to the tactics misinformation makers commonly use to build resistance. The other is lateral reading: teaching people to leave the original page and verify the organization's background via trusted sources (including Wikipedia) when they encounter an unfamiliar information source, much as a fact-checker would.

14:09 Searching online tricks you into thinking you actually understand
A 2023 study found that people who searched the internet for answers to questions like 'Why do we have leap years?' or 'How do zippers work?' reported greater confidence they could explain those things than people who simply read given materials. Yet when actually asked to explain, the search group was less accurate. Psychologist Tania Lombrozo calls this the 'illusion of understanding': finding information doesn't equal actually understanding it. Her suggested remedy is simple: force yourself to say it aloud or write it down, which will expose what you actually know and don't know.

15:10 Critical thinking grows through struggle, not through getting answers
Lombrozo is direct: friction in learning is beneficial. Methods that feel difficult and slow—self-testing, recalling from memory, spacing out study sessions, working through problems yourself—generally work better than methods that seem easier (passively rereading notes, searching, asking AI). She also cautions parents and teachers against too quickly handing over answers or solutions, because part of developing critical thinking happens in the struggle itself. Negron takes a broader view: he argues the real solution isn't any single classroom technique but better, more rigorous education for everyone—including teaching the public how to understand AI itself and controversial topics like vaccines. This requires sustained investment over decades, not one-off experimental interventions.

item.title: Socrates proves: the deliberate wrongdoer is superior to the unwitting one

item.content:encoded:
This conclusion inverts legal intuition—normally, intentional wrongs draw harsher penalties than negligent ones—yet using running, a lame foot, and a lost helmsman, Socrates leads listeners step-by-step to the opposite: that deliberate wrongdoing makes a person superior.

The latter half's Ion argument about inspiration versus technical craft remains directly applicable to today's creators; the earlier section's sophistry demands patience to trace where each step performs its conceptual substitution.

2:03 The deliberate wrongdoer is superior to the unwitting one
Socrates states his essay's core claim: anyone who intentionally commits injustice, speaks falsehood, or deceives is actually superior to someone who does these unwittingly. Hippias had tried defending Achilles by saying he ‘merely changed his mind, not deliberately lied’—but this actually handed Socrates his weapon. ‘Changing his mind’ reveals that Achilles lacks a stable disposition, which becomes the argument's real hinge. Socrates flips the proposition: deliberate wrongdoing proves you at least have the capacity to act otherwise; unwitting wrongdoing means you lack even the power to choose.

3:05 Fast equals good: this premise hides the trap
Socrates opens with what seems like harmless common sense: a good runner is one who runs fast, a bad runner is one who runs slow—reducing ‘good’ to a concrete quality (speed). This appears merely definitional, yet it becomes the anchor for the entire argument. Once ‘good equals some technical standard’ is locked in, the next move becomes possible: which runner is actually ‘better’—one who intentionally runs slow, or one who accidentally runs slow? The answer is the intentional one, because intentionality proves he has the capacity to run fast but simply chooses not to. This reasoning collapses ‘being skilled at doing X’ into ‘being able to deliberately do X well or badly’—and that collapse prepares the path for all the analogies about body parts, tools, and ultimately the soul itself.

14:18 From a lame foot to the soul: an absurd logical chain
The argument branches outward from running to feet, eyes, helmsmen, horses, bows, archers, and finally to the soul. Each step treats body parts and tools as if their ‘goodness’ hinges on whether they can be controlled by intention. A foot that is deliberately lame is better than one that is lame by accident. An eye that deliberately sees poorly is superior to an eye with accidental poor vision. Own a horse you deliberately ride badly—and your soul is superior. The logic marches forward with mechanical precision: every tool, every body part, every faculty becomes subject to the same test. As the hosts acknowledge, the reasoning chain is absurd, but precisely because it's so rigorously absurd, it rewards careful attention to where exactly each step performs a conceptual sleight of hand.

18:32 This absurd reasoning might be a proof by contradiction
The hosts propose a crucial reinterpretation: perhaps Plato never meant this whole chain—from ‘fast is good’ to ‘a soul that deliberately errs is superior’—as his actual position. Instead, it could be reductio ad absurdum, a logical trap designed to support what Socrates genuinely believes: that no one ever knowingly does evil. The hidden flaw is an equation between techne (craft) and arete (virtue). In the world of craft, you can decouple capacity from action—you have the skill to run fast but choose to run slow. But in virtue, knowledge and character are inseparable; genuine understanding of the good cannot coexist with deliberately doing wrong. Hippias piles craft upon craft but cannot thereby construct an intact soul or coherent virtue—the whole exceeds the sum of its parts.

23:47 Why Homer's expert cannot answer about Hesiod
Ion, a rhapsode, claims he is the master of Homer and can answer any question about Homer's poetry—yet the moment you ask him about Hesiod or other poets, he grows drowsy and silent. Socrates sets the trap: if Ion has truly mastered Homer as a unified subject, he must equally command all the technical knowledge Homer discusses—medicine, chariot-racing, military strategy—because mastering a subject means mastering all its contents. But Ion plainly doesn't. Worse, there is no single unified craft of ‘poetry’ to master in the first place. Socrates' conclusion: Ion's talent isn't knowledge but divine possession—inspiration that flows like a chain of iron rings attracted to a magnet: the god possesses the poet, the poet possesses the rhapsode, the rhapsode possesses the audience.

40:16 When Homer writes of fishing, let the fisherman judge
The hosts cite Homer's description of bait sinking into the sea. The question cuts to the heart of the matter: whose craft—the rhapsode's or the fisherman's—gives authority to say whether Homer's account is accurate and well-described? Clearly the fisherman's. This example crystallizes Ion's deeper problem: if a rhapsode is to judge every specialized detail Homer writes about using a single unified craft, he'd need to master fishing, chariot-driving, warfare, and every other domain Homer touches. But no single person can acquire all these skills. This proves that ‘the craft of commenting on Homer’ does not exist as a unified expertise. Ion's gift is closer to performance and emotional transmission than to professional verification—not checking whether Homer got his facts right, but conveying feeling.

46:23 Better to claim divine possession than admit you were wrong
Cornered, Ion suddenly proclaims himself not merely Greece's finest rhapsode but also Greece's finest general—he learned it all from Homer's epics. Socrates presses: if so, why has no one asked you to command troops? Ion first invokes political obstacles, then claims it's because he's a foreigner. Socrates calmly recites a list of foreign commanders who did get appointed, sealing that escape route. At the dialogue's end comes the final thrust, disguised as graciousness: Socrates offers Ion a choice—how would you rather be known: as a liar, or as someone divinely possessed? Ion chooses divine possession. He doesn't realize it's a trap that demolishes his claim to any craft whatsoever—he's just repackaged his lack of knowledge in language that sounds noble.

50:28 Teaching people to think freely is itself a form of force
The discussion extends to Socrates' stance in the Republic on censoring poetry. If poets are merely vessels of divine inspiration who don't understand what they're saying, then allowing ordinary people unfiltered access to myths saturated with jealousy and treachery will corrupt them. The hosts push back: education should cultivate citizens' own capacity to filter and judge culture, not impose top-down censorship. But then they catch themselves in a paradox: education itself is top-down force—children don't consent to being taught critical thinking. ‘Teaching people to become independent thinkers’ happens through means that aren't themselves free. The paradox doesn't dissolve, only surfaces. There's no clean resolution, just the tension laid bare.
